title: Newton's First Law
learning_goal: Explain equilibrium and inertia using Newton's First Law.

stages.title: 1. Newton's First Law
stages.content: An object remains at rest or continues moving at constant velocity unless acted on by a net external force. This tendency to resist a change in motion is called inertia.

stages.title: 2. Inertia and mass
stages.content: Mass is a measure of inertia. An object with greater mass is harder to speed up, slow down, or redirect than an object with less mass.

stages.title: 3. Equilibrium
stages.content: When the net force on an object is zero, the object is in equilibrium. It may be at rest or moving at constant velocity.

stages.title: 4. Worked example
stages.content: A book rests on a table. Gravity pulls downward while the table's normal force pushes upward with equal magnitude. The net force is zero, so the book remains at rest.

stages.title: 5. Guided practice
stages.prompt: A hockey puck slides across nearly frictionless ice at constant velocity. What does Newton's First Law tell you about the net force on the puck?
stages.hint: Constant velocity means the motion is not changing.
stages.alternate_explanation: If the puck is neither speeding up, slowing down, nor turning, its acceleration is zero. Zero acceleration means the forces are balanced.

stages.title: 6. Mastery check
stages.content: To demonstrate mastery, identify examples of inertia, distinguish balanced from unbalanced forces, explain equilibrium, and predict motion when the net force is zero.

concept_cards.title: Newton’s first law describes unchanged velocity
concept_cards.content: In an inertial reference frame, an object remains at rest or continues in a straight line at constant velocity when its net external force is zero. The law concerns velocity, so turning counts as a change even if speed stays constant.

concept_cards.title: Balanced forces are not absent forces
concept_cards.content: A book on a table has downward weight and an upward normal force. Their equal magnitudes and opposite directions give zero net force. Draw all forces on the chosen object before deciding whether they balance.

visual.label: A book at rest: equal upward normal force and downward weight act on the same object.

concept_cards.title: Inertia is a property measured by mass
concept_cards.content: Inertia describes resistance to a change in velocity. Greater mass means greater inertia. Inertia is not a force, and motion does not need to be used up. A force is needed to change velocity.

concept_cards.title: Everyday friction can hide the pattern
concept_cards.content: A sliding box slows because the floor exerts friction. That does not mean constant motion requires a continuous forward force. It means the box does not satisfy the zero-net-force condition. On ideal frictionless ice, an object can continue moving without a forward push.

concept_cards.title: A passenger during braking
concept_cards.content: Relative to the road, the passenger tends to retain the previous forward velocity as the car slows. Relative to the slowing car, the passenger moves forward until a restraint or another interaction changes that motion. A seat belt provides the force that slows the passenger.

worked_examples.prompt: A book rests on a horizontal table. Which statement describes the forces on the book?
choices: The upward normal force balances downward weight
worked_examples.answer: The upward normal force balances downward weight
accepted_answers: The upward normal force balances downward weight
hint_steps: Identify the object and decide whether its velocity changes.
Does being at rest mean no forces exist, or that their sum is zero?
worked_examples.alternate_explanation: Gravity pulls the book downward and the table exerts an upward normal force. They balance on this book, giving zero net force. These two forces are not a Newton’s-third-law pair because both act on the same object.
alternate_explanation_steps: Choose an inertial reference frame, such as a stationary classroom or road for these examples.
Zero net external force means zero acceleration. Velocity can be zero or a nonzero constant.
Does being at rest mean no forces exist, or that their sum is zero?

solution_steps.explanation: A book rests on a horizontal table. Which statement describes the forces on the book?

Gravity pulls the book downward and the table exerts an upward normal force. They balance on this book, giving zero net force. These two forces are not a Newton’s-third-law pair because both act on the same object.

solution_steps.equation: The upward normal force balances downward weight
solution_steps.explanation: Apply the zero-net-force condition; do not confuse speed, velocity, inertia, and force.

worked_examples.prompt: A car brakes suddenly. Why does an unrestrained passenger tend to continue forward relative to the car?
choices: Braking creates a new forward force
The passenger tends to retain the previous velocity while the car slows
worked_examples.answer: The passenger tends to retain the previous velocity while the car slows
accepted_answers: The passenger tends to retain the previous velocity while the car slows
hint_steps: Identify the object and decide whether its velocity changes.
What interaction would change the passenger’s forward velocity?
worked_examples.alternate_explanation: In a road-based frame, the passenger tends to continue with the previous forward velocity while the car slows. A seat belt supplies a backward force that slows the passenger. No new forward force is needed to explain this relative motion.
alternate_explanation_steps: Choose an inertial reference frame, such as a stationary classroom or road for these examples.
Zero net external force means zero acceleration. Velocity can be zero or a nonzero constant.

conceptual_questions.prompt: Explain why a puck can keep moving without a continuing forward push on ideal frictionless ice.
expected_ideas: Zero net force means velocity remains unchanged, not that velocity must be zero.
misconceptions: Motion always needs a continuous force in its direction.
conceptual_questions.follow_up: What would be needed to change the puck’s velocity?

conceptual_questions.prompt: Explain why a passenger tends to move forward relative to a suddenly braking car, and how a seat belt changes that motion.
expected_ideas: The passenger tends to retain the earlier forward velocity while the car slows.
The seat belt supplies a force that slows the passenger; inertia is not a forward force.
misconceptions: Braking produces a new forward force on the passenger.
conceptual_questions.follow_up: Which interaction changes the passenger’s velocity?

conceptual_questions.prompt: A book is at rest on a table. Explain why “no force acts on the book” is incorrect.
expected_ideas: Weight acts downward and a normal force acts upward.
They balance on the book, so net force is zero even though individual forces exist.
misconceptions: An object at rest cannot have forces acting on it.
conceptual_questions.follow_up: What two objects interact with the book?
